utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. Absent amongst the Defence teams are the following: Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Krgovic, and that's it. The witness is here. Professor Dunjic, good morning to you. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll finish with your testimony today. I don't know. I don't promise, but we'll try. Mr. Gosnell. You've finished? Yes. We had finished Mr. Gosnell. We had finished Ms. Nikolic. So it's Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President, I have a couple of short questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic, and I represent General Miletic. I would now like to ask you a few questions on Potocari. Yesterday, you stated that on the basis of the report it was impossible to establish the moment of death. I am interested in the following: During the autopsy, was it possible to establish the time of death using methods?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, during the autopsy that was not possible to establish nor was it possible during the exhumation, but during the exhumation and during the autopsy it was necessary to describe various elements which would have helped us to determine more precisely the time of death such as the changes on the corpse, et cetera. These are the elements missing in these autopsy reports, and it's from these elements that we indirectly find out approximately the time of death or the time of burial. Those are two things, the time of burial and the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Today, on the basis of the elements which you have and which are in these reports, you cannot tell us at all when -- if it was in 1992, 1993, 1995, the people died, the moment of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, based on this I cannot make that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing from us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Mitchell. How long do you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I hope less than an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Then, please make sure that the next witness is here as soon as we finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to start out and ask you a couple of questions about the examination from my friend from the Nikolic team yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, and if you need to -- the gentleman you've been referring to and others that we need to be in private session, please be careful. Draw our attention, and we'll go back in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I want to read you a paragraph on this page and then get your comments on it. Under the second bullet point, it says: "ICMP anthropologists do not engage in identification of human remains. They assist local authorities with exhumations and prepare remains for DNA testing. ICMP would like to ensure that remains are buried only once DNA testing has been completed. Especially in the early days, however, ICMP and local authorities were not always able to ensure that remains are buried following DNA testing only. As a consequence, re-exhumations have become necessary, in particular where a missing person is recovered and identified as someone whom family members believe they have already buried." Now, Professor, are you familiar with this situation described here where an error is made in the anthropological identification and it's then later corrected through DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is mentioned in that text several times, only I have a comment about this in case you care to hear it. Anthropologists have a very significant role in the verification, not only in the preparation of samples for DNA identification. I said it yesterday, and I'll repeat it now: Identification is a complex process in which the DNA analysis is the crown of all that must be done. But it is not an untouchable, undoubtable proof because errors can be made in the extraction and the storage, et cetera, and also in the interpretation of the DNA profile. So in order to make a complete analysis, you need the forensic aspect, the anthropological aspect, and the genetic aspect, so that I do not fully agree with the ICMP in that sentence about anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, in 1998 you supervised exhumations at Lake Radonjic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you and three of your colleagues -- well, 39 bodies were recovered from this site, correct -- I mean, a minimum of 39 bodies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you and your colleagues identified 12 of these bodies by anthropological methods, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the DNA analysis later showed that three of these identifications were incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Can I comment, though, and reply to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- since I'm the living proof of the fact that incomplete identification can lead to wrong conclusions. I was head of the team making an anthropological analysis and other analyses, but we had still to do DNA analysis. So we had to extract samples for DNA analysis. This was all in the summer of 1998. If you apply the classical identification method, apart from anthropological and forensic aspects, you need to take samples from the nearest of kin. So you need ante-mortem data that go to show what kind of person that was, how he or she was dressed, how tall he or she was, and other anthropological characteristics, which information must be matched to what you find in the field. But the problem with the remains of the clothes was that the relatives gave wrong information, or they misidentified some clothes; and the greatest problems was with Albanians who wouldn't and weren't allowed to testify as to some of their near relative died. So based on the information that some relative recognized a piece of clothing, we identified an individual as being X or Y, but it turned out that we made some mistakes, and we were aware of it at the time. So -- and I repeat that identification based on anthropological information is very sensitive. We made no forensic mistakes. We were very precise. But some details that were essential - in this case it was DNA - led us to correct our conclusions so that -- and the example of the possibility of making mistakes. So why am I telling you that? I went to Madrid with the representative of the Prosecution to transport some samples, and what is mentioned in this letter - I mean the personnel we referred to - we were taking samples to Madrid to make an analysis, and the samples of bones that were found in Batajnica, for those we got profiles right away. The samples from the case that you referred to, they were stored in plastic bags and refrigerated, and so they decayed, and -- so there was accelerated decay due to the circumstance in Belgrade at the time. And in Madrid, they were not able to determine the DNA samples. And those samples from Madrid, once we learned about it, we had to re-exhume all the corpses that were found in Kosovo, and only then was a correct profile made. That was the whole story why a mistake was made in the identification. So that I'm very familiar with that. The DNA profile we saw yesterday is the DNA profile of a bone from the electropherogram, and that is very important. The electropherogram enables you to make an accurate DNA profile. You now remember those peaks I pointed out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So based on your experience, you'd agree that DNA-matching is an integral part of the identification process that started with the anthropological and forensic examination of the remains?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That's the right thing to do. That would be the true identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, let's move to a different area. I'd like to talk to you about the graves in Potocari that you were asked some questions about yesterday. There are three known graves in Potocari, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There is one behind the zinc factory, which was assumed in 2004; there's one which was exhumed in the Rabin field in 2005; and a second grave exhumed in the Rabin field in 2006, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, you can go ahead now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to clarify with you the exact location of these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can I please have in e-court 65 ter 3894. That's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, what you're about to see is a sketch done by an RS MUP crime technician of the 2005 exhumation site in the Rabin field. If we can just scroll down a little bit. As you can see on the sketch, the site is located approximately 27 metres from the Budak road and 3 metres away from the stream on the left-hand side of the field. Now, yesterday you confirmed that there were three bodies exhumed from this grave in 2005, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And these bodies are labeled SR-POT-01/1, 2, and 3?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have in e-court 65 ter 3895?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, what you're going to see here is another sketch done by an RS MUP crime technician which shows the site of the 2006 exhumation in the Rabin field. Now, the exhumation report for this site which you reviewed for your report actually had the incorrect coordinates written on it. The correct coordinates are written on the sketch, and these have been verified by a Prosecution investigator who went to that site. So looking at this sketch, you can see that the second grave is 29 metres from the road and 6 metres in from the stream. Can you see that? So you can tell from these measurements that this grave is within a couple of metres of the one that was exhumed in 2005, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more to the north, I would say. I actually don't know where east is, where north is. This is 29 and this is 27, so it would be one on top of the other or one above the other if -- that's how they were positioned, one on top of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there were ten sets of remains exhumed from this site in 2006, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not ten bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Ten sets of --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there were six men and one woman [Realtime transcript read in error, "six women"]. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified yesterday that only one of these sets of remains mentioned any evidence of injury in the autopsy report, correct? That was case number 7.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there was only such an expression -- a description, i.e., of the presence of an injury that might but only might correspond to a wound inflicted by a firearm. We are talking about number 7, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's just to correct the transcript. Page 13, line 8, one reads, "there were six men and six women", and this is not exactly what the witness said. Could the witness perhaps repeat his answer concerning the number of bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Professor -- thank you, Ms. Fauveau. Can you follow-up on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six men. Thank you. Six men, one woman. That's what I said, and that's how it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we please look at 65 ter number 4D00540.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this is your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 38 in the English and page 20 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, this is the autopsy report for the remains labeled POT 01 SRE 001. Now, under the heading "Other Observations," the autopsy reports significant trauma to this body, including damage to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossa of the right scapula. Now, that damage isn't identified as post-mortem damage, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please, when we're talking about D, it says evidence of injury, and it says none under that, which means that there is no evidence of injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, and then it says "Other Observations." Under that, it says PM damage to the distal ends of the left clavicle; damage and effects to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus scapula fossa, P; and damage to the anterior and posterial ends of the ribs bilaterally; and let me not go on reading the rest of the observations. So the other observations marked as PM is just a list of the things that were observed and that could be explained or accounted for as post-mortem injuries, e.g., after the death. These were not considered proofs of injury, and they could not establish even with a lesser extent of reliability what the cause of death was, and let me just finish. When you read this under "Other Observations," and if we go back to the previous case of which you have asked me and for which you have witnesses that the person had committed suicide - and I won't mention the name of the person who hanged himself - in the same paragraph of the post-mortem record under "Other Observations," you will see very similar descriptions of damages and defects, which means that it was done by one and the same person in the same way and that damages and defects were described very inconsistently. That's why we are unable to draw any conclusions, any final conclusions, and that's what I've been claiming all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, it was a simple question. That damage to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossa isn't listed as post-mortem damage, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very possible. However, I'm not aware of the nature of the damage. I am not aware of the nature of the defect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There is no indication there, is there, Professor? There is no -- nothing there that says post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says PM. PM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But it doesn't say PM on the line that describes damage to the right scapula, does it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this PM, I provided a comment on that in my written report. There is nothing to describe here as being ante-mortem or post-mortem if you're dealing with a skeleton. I will accept this as it has been written, as PM. However, the line that you have just read out where the abbreviation PM is missing, this abbreviation, PM, does not accompany every sentence. However, this is a description that means nothing. Just the word "damage" doesn't mean a thing. It's as if I were to say, for example, that we all have pencils on our tables as -- and you are supposed to take that as a fact. However, I have a ballpoint pen, some have other things, and some don't have pencils at all. So this is a general term which this person used and was not supposed to use. This is something that should not be used in forensic science. If you consider the word "defect," how would you explain that to the judges? I know what a defect is. It can be a skin defect. It can be a bone defect. It has its surface. It has its borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. I think the essence of any testimony, examination-in-chief and cross-examination is to make sure that we stick to what is relevant and we do it in a concise way and that we are all able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff. I don't think we have been doing this, so from now on - especially Professor, I am addressing myself to you in particular - if you expand beyond what is barely necessary or if you, Mr. Mitchell, together with the witness concentrate on matters that we feel are not that important or relevant, we will be drawing your attention and directing you to cut it short. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I just have one more question about this autopsy report. Under the heading "Samples Taken," it lists a projectile, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says "projectiles," plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't want to go through all the other reports from this site, but I want to briefly summarise some of the findings for you. The autopsy reports for POT 01 SRE 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9 all describe trauma under the heading "Other Observations" in the autopsy report, and they all describe at least some trauma that is not listed as post-mortem. In addition, under the heading "Samples Taken," projectiles are listed in each of those autopsy reports that I've just named. So, Professor, isn't it fair to say that each of these autopsy reports actually does describe significant trauma to the remains; it's just not listed under the heading "Evidence of Injury"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Professor, before you answer. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an observation to make. I'm not sure that the witness should stay here while we are discussing this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If I recall, Professor Dunjic does understand English. Is that correct? Yes, he did does. So I think you need to leave the courtroom for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, here one starts from the presumption that the projectile was -- if you look at the autopsy report, one sees, indeed, that the samples taken, colon, and then the projectiles, colon, hyphen, it means I think there were none; and then after that, you got again -- it says here "ADN has been taken," and then the rest will -- I'm not at all sure that the projectiles have been found and taken on the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam. Do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's under the heading "Samples Taken." I think the clear implication is that this is a sample that's taken from the body. In any event, the question I put to Professor Dunjic was just asking him to confirm that that was actually written under the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can leave it at that, and then we see, basically. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's bring Professor Dunjic back, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience and understanding, Professor. We are proceeding, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, my last question was: Isn't it fair to say that in each of the autopsy reports that I just described, it actually does describe significant trauma to the remains; it's just not listed under the heading "Evidence of Injury." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct, first of all. Not completely. You can't say that they sustained those injuries. In the chapter evidence of injury it says, loud and clear, none. And then after that, there is a sub-chapter entitled "Other Observations," so there is no evidence of injury on the one hand and there are injuries on the other hand, and the person lists fractures, defects, on various bones. They were -- are not described according to any standards. There is no mechanism of injury, and he doesn't put them in the group entitled "Evidence of Injury." These are merely his observations, the things that he saw; and from that, he arrived at a conclusion that the cause of death cannot be established. This is the consistency between the conclusion and the findings that I've already spoken about. And as for the samples taken, and it says "Projectiles," semi-colon, dash, I've already explained that. It doesn't say whether 1, 2, 3, 4, or more projectiles were found in which part of the body, in which of the bones, and there is no evidence of the projectile penetration either on the clothes or on the bones. This is nothing but a form which is printed and copied, one of the entries is "Samples Taken," "Projectiles," so if you find them as a doctor, you just say that projectiles were found, and you may even add to that how many were found. And this is the way you should understand this report or findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. There were ten sets of remains that were found at this site in 2006, and yesterday you testified that the autopsy reports showed seven actual bodies, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So just to summarise this information on the Rabin field graves, Professor: We had three graves exhumed in 2005, and in 2006 an additional six bodies have been identified. So that's a total of nine bodies from this area of the Rabin field, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back to that to see whether there were six or nine. In addition to the six identifications, the other two would make up seven, seven and eight were reassociated, so I suppose it was nine. Your Honours, I've never had this document when I prepared my analysis, this document showing DNA identifications. I had post-mortem reports which state that the skull marked by number 5 is a female skull, and that was all. However, if the DNA matching was done and reassociation with the bones and the case is taken as 003, then it is just person. And this only confirms something that I've already said, and that is that the information in the post-mortem reports are totally non-transparent; and for me as pathologist, forensic pathologist, I can't confirm that. I have to reject this. And then you give me a DNA matching report, which says that it was not two bodies but just one, so the whole process of exhumations and identification is now being questioned. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I just want to confirm the numbers with you. It was three bodies exhumed in 2005, and after you've seen this DNA matching report, we now know there were six individuals exhumed in 2006. And that's a total of nine bodies, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2006, there was a total of ten skeletal remains; and in 2005, there were three skeletal remains. In 2004, there was just one skeletal remains in the Potocari location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday my friend from the Borovcanin Defence team told you about six individuals who died or were killed in the DutchBat compound and whose remains are unaccounted for. He then asked you if there was anything in the forensic material that would exclude the possibility that those six individuals were buried in the Rabin field graves. Do you remember that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to put a different situation before you based on facts in this case, and we discussed this briefly last time you were here, but I want to give you a little bit -- a few more details this time. Now, we've heard testimony in this case from two United Nations officers, Koster and Rutten, who saw nine bodies with gunshot wounds next to a stream in Potocari on 13 July 1995. A third DutchBat officer, PW114, described seeing nine to ten bodies in the same area on the same date. Now, all three of these officers gave evidence that the individuals had been shot in the back. Now, Professor, an injury to one or both scapula or to the ribs, that would be consistent with that testimony, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That such injuries were found during the autopsy of the bodies or if these were found, that would be consistent with that statement. But there simply are no injuries to those body parts that could stem from gunshot wounds. There are no such injuries, and therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have in e-court 65 ter 3482.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, what we're about to see is an area of the Rabin field which was taken on 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It might actually make more sense if we turn the picture upside down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, if you recall the sketches of the Rabin field graves that we looked at earlier, you can recognise the Budak road running along the bottom of the picture. The stream is concealed in that line of trees, just to the left of centre, and that's the Rabin field itself in the centre of the picture. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 3483 in e-court, please. Now, if we can turn this one upside down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this is an aerial of the Rabin field from 27 July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, can we turn it upside down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, sometime between 17 and 27 July, two areas of disturbed earth appeared in the Rabin field. Now, if you remember where the sketches of those two graves were located, you will see that that one area to the left of your screen is the same area where the nine bodies were exhumed in 2005 and 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, can I please in e-court 65 ter number 3897, and I actually have hard copies of these. If I can give one to the witness and four to the Bench. It's also in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this is a compilation of aerials of the Rabin field which were put together by a Prosecution investigator. Now, the larger image shows that area of disturbed earth which appeared between 17 and 27 July. The three smaller images were taken from aerials marked by those three DutchBat witnesses to show the spot where they saw nine or ten bodies on 13 July; and just to clarify, on the larger image the investigator placed those marks there just to highlight the spot, the places marked by those DutchBat witnesses. So to summarise this information, we have witnesses -- three witnesses who saw nine to ten bodies next to a stream in Potocari on 13 July 1995. They all testified that the bodies had gunshot wounds to the back. Now, sometime between 17 and 27 July, an area of disturbed earth appeared in the Rabin field within metres of where those DutchBat witnesses saw the nine or ten bodies. Then in 2005 and 2006, we have nine bodies exhumed from the same area. Professor, could this information assist you in determining what happened to the nine individuals who were exhumed from the Rabin field graves in 2005 and 2006?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise again. The DNA identification that you showed in private session, how many bodies were identified there as a total? Because I have the identification of six persons, and I don't know if those are bones of the arm, but that doesn't amount to a total of nine by any means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, there were six bodies identified in 2006, and as you'll recall, in 2005 there were a further three bodies exhumed from a site right next to that one. So it's the three plus the six equals nine.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. So you are adding up what was exhumed in 2006 and 2005. All right. So could you please put your question again with regard to these sketches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. As I said, we have three witnesses who saw nine or ten bodies in this area. They testified that the bodies had gunshot wounds to the back; an area of disturbed earth appeared between 17 and 27 July; and then in 2005 and 2006, a total of nine bodies is exhumed from that area. And my question was: Could this information assist you in determining what happened to those nine individuals who were exhumed in 2005 and 2006?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement they made can point to nine persons who suffered gunshot wounds. That is a realistic assumption. For that realistic assumption to be considered evidence in court, it must be accompanied with autopsy reports to corroborate that; and we are talking about two things, three persons and six persons found at two different sites, albeit close, but two sites nonetheless, which points toward two inhumations or burials. Out of these persons that I haven't seen the autopsy reports for three, but I reviewed in detail the reports for the other six, in none but one case, number 7, I have found the description of an injury that would be consistent with inflicting a gunshot wound, inflicting a gunshot wound. That is reason for me to doubt things in my witness statement. And the clothing remains for -- on these bodies and from 2005 and 2006, so the description of that clothing does not include damage done by a projectile. And then, obviously, the anthropological analysis here is highly suspect because an error was made, for example, in determining the gender of an individual whose skull was found. And this, in my observation, when I say that this was completely untransparent and actually unusable and superficially drafted, is now again confirmed. And the statements of the witnesses who saw that cannot be matched with the forensic findings. So the forensic findings cannot confirm their statements. I have nothing here to confirm the statements of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify. There's a second area of disturbed earth you can see on that image. My information is that that area has been probed and nothing has been found, so just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to move to a different area now and talk about the Sandici grave, which you analysed in your report. Now, as you told us in 2004, a grave was exhumed at Sandici which contained 17 sets of remains, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And I am finished with this document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions about your analysis of the Sandici grave. Professor, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence in this case that on the evening of 13 July 1995, a group of 10 to 15 Muslim men were executed at the Sandici meadow, executed by members of the RS Special Police brigade from the Jahorina training centre. Now, the witness who testified about this execution stated that some of these witnesses were executed with bursts of fire and others with a shot to the head. Now, last time you testified here, you told us that this kind of information could be very important for your analysis. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That is para -- medical information that can help me in choosing a direction for establishing the manner of inflicting injury. When I got that information, I look for data in the autopsy report confirming that there were injuries as sustained from bursts of fire or shots to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And were you provided with this information when you were asked to analyse the autopsy reports from the Sandici grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autopsy reports, I didn't find such information except in three cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor. You misunderstood my question. I'm asking, were you provided with the information about this the witness's testimony when you were asked to analyse the autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the grave we've just discussed, there are six sets of surface remains that were found in the Sandici area, correct? There were three sets in 2000, one set in 2001, one in 2002, and then one in 2005, and that's in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Uh-huh. [Interpretation] And that was contained in the documents that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we're about to look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter number 3609 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, what we're about to see, Professor, it's that document from the Federal Commission for Missing Persons dated 28 December 2007, which contains information on all the surface remains found between 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Is there an English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's not released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this -- yes, you'll recall from your review that this contains information on all the surface remains --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- between 1996 --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 3 of this letter, and there should be a translation in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, this letter shows that between 1996 and 2007, a total of 929 sets of surface remains were collected in the area from Ravni Bujan to Nezuk and the surrounding areas, correct? I just need an answer for the transcript, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this. I know. I know exactly. I know this document exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And there's 484 of these remains have been identified, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were identified, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in the surface remains update there were three people who were reported missing in 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we can agree that the death of those three individuals is not related to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went missing in 1993, and they are on this list of surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in your report you've identified a further 19 individuals who went missing in August 1995, 3 in September 1995, and 2 in October 1995; and you suggested that these are not connected with the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware that following the fall of Srebrenica, groups of Muslim men remained for weeks and sometimes months in the woods in Serbian territory while they were attempting to get to Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And are you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, so you're not aware that specific evidence in this case that Muslim men that were still being captured by Bosnian Serb forces until at least mid-November 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is not known to me. I'm a forensic expert. I did not have an opportunity to read anything of the kind. I quoted the statements to which I referred in my previous reports -- report submitted here, and I referred to events that took place in that period, no more than that. I don't know about any other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I just have one more quick area I'd like to cover in respect of surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please 65 ter 3902 in e-court, and it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Professor, there's not a translation of this document. It was a short information report that was prepared yesterday by a Prosecution investigator, just to update this information in the surface remains document. Now, it's the Prosecution's position that to date, 620 Srebrenica-related individuals have been identified from that total of 929 surface remains cases that were collected between 1996 and 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask just clarification of the term "Srebrenica-related"? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Referring to people who went missing in July, August, September, October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, let's proceed now, and it's time for the break. As soon as Professor Dunjic answers this question, we'll go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have just a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I just wanted to very quickly work through this number of 620 with you just so the Court and everybody understands where it came from. Now, in the surface remains update that we just looked at, there were 484 individuals. We subtracted the three individuals who were reported missing in 1993, which leaves us with 481. The investigator who drafted this report then identified 139 individuals in the ICMP's 2008 update, and he identified them as surface remains based on their case ID, which corresponded with data in that surface remains update. So the 481 individuals in the update plus the 139 individuals from the ICMP update equals 620 identified individuals out of that total of 929 surface remains cases. In your view, does that help clarify this issue of surface remains and the numbers of Srebrenica-related individuals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is logical that the bodies would be scattered all over the place, on the surface, in the woods, in the fields during war. It's only logical, as I say, and I can fully appreciate that, why they were scattered and found like that. The circumstances which led to their death is something that can only be shown by forensic pathology findings, and without that you cannot establish the time of death without an autopsy. I don't know who these people are. You're showing me the extended list, i.e., the document with that list, and I can only say that these persons were found under various circumstances. Now, whether these circumstances were tied to Srebrenica or some other cases that took place before the 11th of July around Srebrenica which is very significant, before the 11th of July or after the 11th of July, I can't say that without an autopsy, i.e., without the time of death being at least approximately established; and this is what I can tell you from my standpoint, from the forensic pathology standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll have about maybe ten minutes after the break. That will be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, there's one final area which I'd like to talk to you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have in e-court 65 ter number 4D00540. That's Professor Dunjic's report, and it's page 140 in the English and page 73 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I want to read you just a small part of your report and then ask you a couple of questions about it. Now, under the heading "Clothes," you say: "At the site in Potocari and the site in Sandici, winter clothes were found on some individuals, which points to the fact that these people died in the winter period before/after the fall of Srebrenica. Another possible conclusion pertaining to the winter clothes discovered at both sites could be a different time of death than stated of persons at the same site and also burial at the same site on several occasions." Now, earlier in your report you described these winter clothes as things such as woollen socks, sweaters, jackets, and leather boots, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was not me saying this. I just quoted from the findings of the physicians who were involved in exhumations and autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I want to show you a few pictures from videos that were taken in Potocari and Sandici on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have in e-court 65 ter 2992. If we can go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this footage was taken in Potocari on 13 July 1995. As you can see, a number of men wearing jackets, sweaters, and what look like woollen hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, my attention is being drawn to the fact that there are some names indicated. I don't know whether those should be protected or not. Out of an abundance of caution, I suppose we proceed out broadcasting. It will be safe enough. So no broadcast of -- and if you are going to make use of names, then we need to check whether we need to be in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, this is also Potocari on 13 July. Again, you can see men wearing jackets, sweaters, and hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This footage was taken in Sandici on the 13th of July. You can see the heavy jacket that's being worn by this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see this man is wearing a jacket and also what appears to be a sweater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go back to one final photo of Potocari on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you can see that the man on the left of this image is holding what appears to be a jacket and he's wearing a red vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, of course, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Is there a re-examination, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have P3485 placed on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Professor, do you remember being asked some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just repeat the exhibit I'm asking for. P3485.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, do you recall being asked some questions about the findings marked on the Potocari autopsy reports that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like to have you take a look at the document on the screen, and this appears to be the autopsy report for POT 01 SRE 006. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me direct --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have page 12 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you see it now, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we now move to page 4 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, what do you see there under Section F?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, how would you -- looking at this, how would you interpret the marking "projectile"? Does it indicate that projectiles were found in or near the remains?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my written report, I've already said that I wasn't clear on this. Under F where it says "Samples Taken," one would imply and one should enter the evidence that was taken during the autopsy, something that was found in the body or on the body during the autopsy. Usually, these would be projectiles or parts thereof or something to that effect. The way things are written here says there were a number of projectiles, plural, with a dash, which means that the form had already contained projectiles as pieces of evidence. So if they are to be found, their number should be listed together with the place where they were found. But this doesn't mean either in this case or in a number of other cases that were projectiles were indeed found. This is just a form of an autopsy report as was prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And to the right of the DNA marking, do you see details which actually describe something relevant to DNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that a sample taken from the body was not a projectile. What was taken was a section of the middle part of the right femur and a tooth. That was what was taken by way of DNA evidence, and then it says "Other Things," nothing was taken. So where it says "projectiles," this is part of the form, but it does not refer to anything that has actually been found either on the body or in the body. That would be my answer to your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if nine individuals had been killed by gunshots, if all of them according to the hypothesis had been killed by gunshots, would you expect to find projectile traces in or near the remains?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the assumption that there had been execution by a burst of fire, as it says here, at a least some fragments of the projectiles would have been found in the tissue, in the bones, in the clothes. At least some of the clothes would have been damaged, and the damages would have been described, but this is missing from these autopsy reports. It hasn't been described. It has not been listed in this report or on the reports describing the nine bodies found in Potocari. And let me digress a little bit further. When you look at the description of the injuries on the bodies who are assumed to have been executed, and if you look at the description of the observations in case Potocari 1/1 whom the witnesses had said that he had hanged himself, you will see that the description is [Realtime transcript read in error, "isn't] identical in all of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand there is a transcription problem at line 15, "is identical."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Gosnell, instead of "isn't."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Professor, it's over. We don't have any further questions for you. I see how pleased you are, being able to return home. Once more, I have the pleasure of thanking you for having come over; and once more, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you too. I may have gone on for a bit long, but I would like to thank you for allowing me to express my expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed. Mr. Gosnell, documents? I see you have only got one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, comments, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Other Defence teams? I hear no comments. Document is admitted. Ms. Nikolic, you have two documents, 515 and 516. Any objections, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no objection to 515, and we have no objection to 516 coming in provided that the ICMP response also comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, do you have any problems with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's problem solved. Any remarks from any of the other Defence teams, Mr. Gosnell or Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No comment from us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So these two documents in addition to the one referred to by Mr. Mitchell, that would -- will accompany 3D00516, forming an integral part of it, are being admitted. Yes, Mr. Mitchell. Prosecution documents? You have 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from the Borovcanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, first of all, Mr. President, if I could just tell you that after looking more closely at the Markovic exhibits, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The four that you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I wish to tell you that first because I would again would request your indulgence to review these documents. There are one or two in particular we may have some concerns with, and I would just -- I need to go back and look and see what's been previously admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll call on you again after the next break. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with regard to 3902 from the OTP list proposed with Professor Dunjic - that's the last document, yes - this is a report that the OTP investigators drafted with an additional list of the identified bodies. I believe that the document in question can -- cannot be admitted through this witness since this is just an information report which compiles the work of the OTP and the demographic department because the compilations are carried out by the demographic department of the OTP based on the ICMP data. That's why I believe that this document should not be admitted through this witness that we have just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before giving you the floor, Mr. Mitchell, let's hear Mr. Haynes, if it's about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It is about the same thing, but can I just crave your indulgence for one second to say on my own behalf and perhaps on behalf of everybody here, to offer my to offer Judge Kwon for his ascension to high office. But I do join that objection. This is a document that was drafted yesterday by somebody called Jans, who hasn't even given it the authority of putting his signature on it. It wasn't addressed with the witness at all. It was simply put on the screen, and then a proposition was put to him. It is debatable whether it has any evidential status whatsoever. If it does have evidential states, then we'll all be running off to ask the court staff, getting them to write short documents stating what our position is on any particular issue in the case, putting them into e-court, and then having them admitted into evidence. It simply has no evidential status whatsoever, and it shouldn't be admitted into evidence. That's P3902 for the avoidance of doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Mitchell, do you insist on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then could you respond to the objection, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was clearly relevant to Professor Dunjic's testimony and his expert report, and the whole aim of this document was to clarify the issue for the Trial Chamber and the Defence, and I think the evidential value of this document is clear on its face. Sorry. It's organising information that's already in evidence and simply clarifying it for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But the point made -- the main point made as far as I am concerned - at least, of course, I need to consult with my colleagues - is that it could be best or better introduced or tendered by or through another witness and not through Professor Dunjic. That's -- because otherwise, the probative value that one attaches is something that will come to -- in due course. In other words, does the testimony of Professor Dunjic give it probative value, make it stronger, or...

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I submit that it clarifies Professor Dunjic's report and his testimony. That's why we showed him this document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- admitting it through Professor Dunjic will save us from calling Investigator Jans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are there objections in the meantime? We hear none, except that you will come later, of course. So what we are going to do is we will postpone the issue until after the break. In the meantime, we'll check whether indeed we do need this document at all in the records, and we'll come to you after the break. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I just briefly add, this was my idea, this document, and I just might be able to provide you some helpful information about why we're offering it, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. President. It's our view that Mr. Dunjic's report was somewhat confusing as was his testimony regarding this issue, of bodies and who was who, and the cross-examination was designed to unravel that. Now, the simplest way for you to see the results from ICMP and the others is through this one-page reorientation of the evidence. This can, of course, be argued by us, can be attached by -- you know, in any brief; but really, it's much like the reorganisation or the organisation of the material that Dean Manning put in just so it can help you make sense of this -- this evidence. This is the kind of thing that by looking at one page you can sort out what this stuff means from the Prosecution's perspective and make a judgment on the issue as opposed to trying to read only the transcript and look for arguments. So it's just a pure simple thing to help your job be easier, which is just based on the evidence that's already in, much like Dean Manning but without having to call the investigator and go over all the material. I don't think there's anything that's contested in there. It's just a brief one-page reorganisation of these key issues related to the bodies, and that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So just to go back to Markovic's documents, did I confirm that the documents on the lists, now having heard Mr. Gosnell, are all admitted or not? No, I haven't, so I'm doing so now. Those documents are admitted. Thank you. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to thank Mr. Haynes for your warm congratulations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Vanderpuye now has joined the team for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start your expert testimony, you are required under our rules to make a solemn declaration that you will be stating the truth and the whole truth. Please read out that text, and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Lazarevic will be putting questions to you. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. I don't see your testimony finishing today, probably not even tomorrow. But -- tomorrow we don't have a sitting, anyway, but probably not even on Friday, although we are having an extended sitting on Friday, although I am going to make an appeal to all parties here to finish by Friday afternoon. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have already had the opportunity to meet, but still for the transcript I must introduce myself to you. I am Aleksandar Lazarevic, and with my colleagues I defend Ljubomir Borovcanin before this Tribunal. A piece of warning -- a warning that I have to give to each witness that speaks the same language as I, after each question please wait for a short while and -- before answering so that there is no overlapping for the transcript; and thus, you will make the interpreter's life easier.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Branislav Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of October, 1982, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A correction: The year is 1972 and not 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. It has been corrected in the transcript. Can you tell me briefly about your education?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Primary school and secondary school, I graduated from Novi Sad, and I completed my law studies at the university in Novi Sad in 1996. I got my masters degree at the same university; and in 2006, I got my doctoral degree at Belgrade university?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have slight problems with the transcript. I believe that this will be resolved. It is probably not necessary to repeat the question. Tell us, please, to which academic positions were you appointed, if any?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed assistant professor in 2007 within Novi Sad university. That is the lowest level academic degree in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Except in teaching and the scholarship, did you also engage in research?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Novi Sad university.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but it seems to me that you reply to my questions too fast, too soon, so that the transcript cannot follow the pace of your reply. So I would just ask you to slow down. You have already told us that you have a doctor's degree, and can you tell us the topic of your dissertation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The topic was crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, for example, some of -- some of your more significant papers?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: My specific field of interest is command responsibility, joint criminal enterprise. That's what I wrote about, and lately I have dealt with the confrontation of legal concepts from the Anglo-saxon tradition and the European continental tradition and their influence on the development of international criminal law and the outcomes of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during your professional work, have you ever been a guest teacher at any other faculties? If so, which? But please wait for this to be recorded in the transcript. You can see it in front of you, so you can adapt the pace of your response.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Last year, I held a short course at the law school of Zagreb University in the framework of their post-graduate studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the topic of that course?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you take part earlier in proceedings before this Tribunal, or were you ever summoned to the international Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a hired by -- as legal assistant by the Defence team of Mr. Krajisnik a number of years ago. Four years ago, I was a member of the state delegation that was here in the procedure for the -- for the extradition of the Kara term 4, so it was an extradition procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we have a problem with the transcript. It was a referral procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's line 8 on page 49, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we have corrected this in the transcript. And the next thing I want to ask you, are you active in politics? Were you at any given moment a member of Serbian parliament?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I used to engage in politics. I was member of Serbian parliament in 2004; and in 2006 and 2007, I was an advisor to the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that you have said that you were advisor of the Serbian prime minister, in which fields did you advise him?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was his legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apart from being a member of parliament, did you at the time hold another position with the parliament of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the head of the justice committee of the Serbian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What did your work in that committee include?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I had -- it included several things, but mostly the -- it was about the opinions to the appointments of judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your curriculum vitae is enclosed. This is Exhibit number 4D504 [Realtime transcript read in error, "4504"]. I will not dwell upon these issues any longer. Tell us now, please, when you -- I apologise, there seems to be a problem with the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is page 50, line 4. It should be 4D504.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will now repeat the question. These problems with the transcript are frequent. When did you first set up contact with the Borovcanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was about a year ago. I must add that the Defence team contacted me and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was said to you at the time about the subject matter of your expertise? What was supposed to be the subject?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was said to me then that the subject of my expertise was the issue of the legal system in force in the Republika Srpska at the time to which the indictment in this case refers. Then, the issues with regard to the changes to that system, when -- when the state of war was declared, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer. I'll read what we have here. You said: "Then the issue with regard to the changes to that system, when a state of war was declared ..." and from then onwards they don't have -- they didn't catch what you said. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Furthermore, the issue of the remit for trying persons for violations of international martial war and the remit with regard to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you accepted to be an expert and when you were appointed, did you have any further contacts with the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met a couple of times in Belgrade after that, and I accepted to draft the expert opinion, and I was provided with all the documents and maybe two or three times after that when I wanted some additional documents from the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you receive the necessary documents which you deemed important for your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, save for some exceptions that I myself could not locate and I could not obtain them from you, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did any members of the Borovcanin Defence team influence you in terms of the contents of your expert opinion or your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to meet Mr. Borovcanin personally, and if you did, could you tell us when and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was towards the end of spring or beginning of summer this year in Bijeljina. That's when I met with the Defence team, and I met Mr. Borovcanin in person. We may have spent five or ten minutes in a conversation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about this. At the moment when you met and saw Mr. Borovcanin, was your expert opinion already drafted and handed in?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the encounter with Mr. Borovcanin that you have just described for us, did you have another occasion to see Mr. Borovcanin, to talk to him? Did you have any other contacts with him after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now I would kindly ask you to tell us, what is it that you have in front of you in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have my own expert opinion, I have documents - those that I used in drafting the opinion - and that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now talk just briefly about the structure of your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 4D503.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the beginning of my expert opinion, you will find the contents, a brief introduction, the indictment, its temporal and spatial framework. I had to investigate the legal system at the time and in the area as defined by the indictment. After that, there is a second part dealing with the relationship between the army of Republika Srpska and the MUP; i.e., the command relationship, i.e., when the MUP of Republika Srpska became part of the armed forces, the way it acted in combat activities. And then there is the third part, the overview and analysis of relevant regulations of the Republika Srpska with a special overview of the change of these regulations in the state of war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could this witness please slow down because this is becoming a bit impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Stop one moment because we were letting you finish. We had the intention to intervene and ask you to slow down, but the interpreters very likely are finding the answers too quick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down. Let's continue. Now, if I may ask the interpreters, do you think you've missed something apart from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, nothing was missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. "Then we had arrived here, and then there is the third part of the interview, analysis with the special overview of the change of these regulations in the state of war ..." Please continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And then there is the fourth part, the issue of the responsibilities of the members of the armed forces for the violations of the humanitarian law and the treatment of prisoners of war; and the fifth part would be the responsibilities and procedures to establish disciplinary and criminal responsibility of the MUP members in war conflicts; and the sixth part would be the conclusions that I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And can we now go to the next page, which is page 2 of your expert opinion. It is the same exhibit that we already have in front of us. You have provided us with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment. Could you please bear with me. Two pages further from here, which is page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your copy, it is page 2. You have provided us with a temporal framework as well as spatial framework which consists with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you determine as the temporal and spatial frameworks of your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The period between March 1995 and November 1995 was my temporal framework. This is the broadest temporal scope that I found in the indictment in paragraphs number 26 and 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the spatial scope of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the spatial scope of the indictment, we are talking about eastern Bosnia or the area which is usually known as the Birca [phoen] region -- or Birac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's continue with the next chapter in your expert report, which is the command relationship between the VRS and the MUP as the components of the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Court to produce exhibit number 4D413. This is the law on the -- application of the Law on Internal Affairs during an imminent threat of war or the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your case, in your binder, it is under tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please look at page 4 in B/C/S and page 12 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
