utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The first article of this law that I would like us to look at is Article 12. Could you please tell us what Article 12 prescribes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Article 12 of this law says that the Ministry of the Interior shall establish special police units to carry out combat tasks, which will complement the special purpose police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we're talking about two types of police units here, and they're both engaged in combat; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the next article, Article 13, which is on the following page of the B/C/S version, and in the English version we can stay on the same page. What I would like to ask you about Article 13 is this: Who is it who issues a -- the order on the use of police units in combat?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Such an order is issued by the Minister [Realtime transcript read in error, "Ministry"] of the Interior pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer because I can see we are having problems with the transcript. Who is it who issues the order on the use of police units in combat?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Such an order is issued by the Ministry of the Interior pursuant to an order issued by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it would be good if we corrected the transcript at one point, page 56, line 5 [as interpreted]. You said "the Minister," not the "Ministry"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now look at paragraph 2 of the same Article 3. Pursuant to this paragraph, who is in charge of the police units and through which bodies? Who is in command of such units, in other words?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior does it through the staff of the police forces command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read that paragraph very slowly to help us have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: "The Minister of the Interior shall control the police units through the ministry police forces command staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It seems that we have a clear record, that everything has been recorded as it should have been. And now, let's move to Article 14 in the same law. First of all, let's look at paragraph 1. Could you please tell me what paragraph 1 provides for and how do you understand it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: According to paragraph 1, the police units which are deployed in combat are resubordinated to the commander of the military unit in whose area of responsibility they will be engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now just briefly, I would like us to move on to another law that you analysed, and we will come back to this one. Let's look what you have under tab 2. That's the Law on Internal Affairs. I would like us to the focus on the part dealing with the use of firearms. This is Article 53 on page 6 in B/C/S and page 14 in the English translation, Article 53, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and the 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 4D212. [Interpretation] We need page 6 in B/C/S and page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have both versions in e-court. Could you tell us, please, what Article 53 of the Law on Internal Affairs prescribes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: According to Article 53, the legality and regularity of the use of coercive means or firearms is being evaluated by authorised officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, who is it who evaluates the justifiability of the use of means of coercion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this article, it would be the minister within seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about this regulation, i.e., the Law on Internal Affairs, are we talking about regular police duties and whether Article 53 applies to such situations?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is about the legality of the use of firearms during normal police work. [Realtime transcript read in error, "Q."]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now, let's go back to 4D413, which is under your tab 1, the Law on the Implication of the Law on Internal Affairs during an imminent threat of war and the state of war, and let's look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been asked to repeat the number of article, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 5 in B/C/S and on page 12 in the English version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What is your comment, or how do you understand the provisions of Article 15 of this law? Is this about the usual procedure that we were able to see in the proceeding regulation or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Under the law on the application of the Law on Internal Affairs in the state of war or, in fact, under Article 15, the assessment of the legality and correctness of the use of firearms is not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So, the provision that we have just been able to see differs essentially from that which is enforced in normal conditions and in the carrying out of normal tasks of the police of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to add that Article 15 clearly stipulates that this refers to the use of firearms and means of coercion in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now that we have seen how the issue of the use of firearms by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be some problems with transcript again. There has been a confusion between question and answer. I'm referring to page 58, line 23 [as interpreted]. This should be the answer rather than the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. All they need to change is the A for a Q, and that will be okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will repeat this last question because I believe you haven't answered it yet. Now that we've had the chance to compare the two regulations regulating the same matter, one in normal conditions and the other in combat operations, can you tell us whether the MUP units that take part in combat operations are still within the regular system of command of the MUP, or are they as part of the armed forces exempt from that system and belong to the other system?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under Article 14, they are resubordinated - I mean the police units - when they engage in combat operations, resubordinated to the commander of the military unit in the area of which they are carrying out a combat task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at Article 16 of this law. It says that members of police units in combat operations have the right to use all weapons and equipment used by the units of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How do you understand Article 16? What is its essence? What does it regulate?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Article 16, its purpose is for police units when they take part in combat operations to be equal in efficiency to military units and to -- or for that to be possible, they must be enabled to use the same kind of weapons as the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In a situation when a unit of the MUP was resubordinated to the commander of the VRS in whose area of responsibility it's carrying out combat tasks, do the rights and authorities of members of the MUP that they normally have change in any way?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under the Law on Internal Affairs, authorised official -- authorised officials of the ministry are those who directly carry out tasks related to public safety and state security. The law on the application of the Law on Internal Affairs in wartime conditions, in the state of war, makes it possible for police units to carry out combat operations, which means that they no longer carry out tasks of public security and state security. Therefore, they no longer have the status granted to authorised officials under the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. When you speak about the law, you mean the law on the application of the Law on Internal Affairs during imminent threat of war or during state of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we speak about combat tasks and when we speak about authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wonder if we could clarify for the record what specific provision of the law we are talking about because there are have been a number of questions just put speaking about the law generally, and I want to know what specific provision the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I must say I am not quite sure what my learned colleague referred to, whether he speaks about law of implementation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I see in the record is the witness answering that under the Law on Internal Affairs, authorised officials in the ministry are those that directly carry out tasks related to public safety and state security. In the following testimony, I don't see a specific reference to the article to which he's referring to in that law. The last we left it was Article 16, which doesn't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. That's Article 35. Here it is. The Law on Internal Affairs, Article 35, paragraph 2. "Those personnel working on operational" -- "carrying out operational tasks and duties related to public and state security are considered authorised officials." I don't think I need to go on reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now look at the following document, 4D337. It's under tab 3 in your binder. Can you tell me what it says?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: First, there is a reference to the legal basis. It says: "Pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander..." That is, the Minister of the Interior issues the following order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one question before we continue with this document. A short while ago, we were able to see the provisions of Article 13 of the law on the implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs during imminent threat of war and in the state of war. If you remember, it regulated -- or it provided for the participation of police units based on the order issued by the Supreme Commander. If we take a look at this order, is it based on the provisions of Article 13 of the said law?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reference in the initial part to the order of the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you spoke about this in more detail in paragraph 2, item 12, of your expert opinion. utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the word "independent" used in item 1 of this order means that the unit is independent from the other units belonging to the Ministry of the Interior. It is now detached.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we continue looking at this order, we see that Mr. Borovcanin was appointed commander of this unit and he was ordered to establish contact with General Krstic, chief of staff of the Drina Corps, upon arriving at his destination. You were able to analyse the document from which it follows that at the time General Krstic commanded the operation for which Mr. Borovcanin was deployed there. How do you understand the obligation of Mr. Borovcanin to report to General Krstic, the commander of the operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand it in line with Article 14 of the law on the implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs in a state of war. That means, as we have already said, that a police unit is resubordinated to the commander of the unit in whose area of responsibility it will engage in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should have a break now.

You're not seeing rawed volumes of material that have been hidden away to be used on cross-examination. These are things that are used specifically to respond to issues that come up, such as the SDS issue. This is not some kind of a mystery material that we are holding back on, and I think it's important that you are able to see this material and accept it for whatever value you think it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please keep yourself as --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'll keep this very short, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The essence of having the expert come here and testify is not to comment upon the entire universe of information that may have been disclosed. It's to comment upon the evidence in the case that's been presented by the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now how this sketch --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL

utterances.text: Enough, enough. Sorry to be so abrupt, but enough.

utterances.text: The third and last objection is to three documents, P3517D. [Realtime transcript read in error]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please, because -- yeah, but it's wrong here. That's why I ask him to repeat.

utterances.text: It's P3517D.

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: P3898D. Sorry, let me take that again. 3898 without a D at the end, just 3898. Now, I do understand the difficulties here, but I hope that the Chamber can understand the difficulties that it poses for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's alarming to me to the hear that argument. It's the same argument I saw in a written submission. utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We've heard enough on this as well. Any other objections? Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gosnell, Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. McCloskey, and Mr. Haynes. Yes, and Mr. Haynes, too, because you associated yourself with Mr. Zivanovic. We start with tendered document 3902. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ristivojevic, there has been a little delay or somewhat longer break than we expected. We had to discuss some procedural matters. I would like to apologise for keeping you waiting. And now, if that's not a problem, I would like to go on and proceed with my examination-in-chief. Before the break, we discussed order number 64/95. Let's look at the following document now. In your binder, it would be under tab 8 -- I apologise. It is your number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exhibit P8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can see that this is an order by the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, dated 22nd April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's look firstly who the addressees of the order are.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The order was sent to the Main Staff of the army and the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now if you'll look at items 1 and 2 of this order, would you say that there were some problems and ambiguities with regard to the engagement of the units of the MUP in -- and their employment in combat?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the letterhead or the heading of the document, there was indeed such ambiguities. It says, We have been informed about some problems and ambiguities -- or rather, confusions regarding the engagement of the MUP in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was ordered to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska with regard to the engagement of the MUP in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff, pursuant to the president's order, has to henceforth define more precisely and concretely their request for the engagement and employment of MUP units in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, and now I believe that we will no longer need this document. And now I would like to ask you something about some other things contained in your expert report. Let's look at the paragraphs starting with 3.1 to 3.32 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are pages 11 through 24 in the e-court system in B/C/S, and in the English those are pages from 9 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me now, before the war broke out in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, what was the division of authorities in the matter of criminal law?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Former Socialist Federative of the Republic of Yugoslavia was a federal state; and when it comes to the matter of criminal law, according to its constitution, the federation had the authority of one part of it, whereas the federal units had authority over a different part of this law. The criminal law of the socialist federative Republic of Yugoslavia regulated the general matters of the criminal law, whereas some groups of the crimes from the special part of the criminal law were also regulated by that. Amongst other things, or rather, this included chapter 16, which referred to crimes against humanity and the international humanitarian law. There was also a special part of the criminal law; i.e., other groups of crimes were left to the federal units, which were the six republics and the two autonomous provinces which had their own special criminal laws. In other words, there were eight criminal laws at the level of the former states, federal units, and there was also one criminal law at the level of the federation itself. Except for the crimes against humanity and the international humanitarian law at the federal level, there were also some other groups of crimes that were provided for by that law. However, these are not important for this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you this: The provisions of the federal criminal law, i.e., the criminal law of the socialist federative Republic of Yugoslavia, were they implemented and applied in all the federal units?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In all the federal units, there was no way to regulate one and the same thing at two levels, i.e., at the level of the federal state and its federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation with the republican, i.e., the provincial criminal laws? In what territories were those implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were in effect only in the territories of those federal units where they were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a very relative -- a very short answer; however, it hasn't been recorded properly. This is page 76, line 17. It seems that the transcript has in the meantime been corrected, and now we have just spoken in very general terms about the system of criminal law and the criminal legislation. This system that we have just spoken about, was it homogenous? Was it harmonized in terms of the provisions of republican provincial laws having had to be in consistency with the federal laws?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The authorities were divided. I've already said that. One thing could not be regulated differently at two different levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now, tell me, please, with regard to the criminal and procedural matters, how were these matters regulated in the former state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the sphere of criminal and procedural law, or rather, the Law on Criminal Procedure, the constitution did not provide for the split of authorities between the federation and its federal units. So there was just one law on criminal procedure which covered the territory of the entire state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about this. In the socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia and its republics and provinces, how was the issue of courts regulated?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were two types of courts. There were regular courts and military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, when the war broke out after the break-up of the socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia, in the system that we have just analysed, were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the state broke up and when the new states emerged in that territory, these new states had two choices. One choice was to pass totally new laws, and the second choice was for them to adopt the laws of the former state, the state that no longer existed. In the sphere of criminal law, most of the new states opted for the latter choice or the latter solution because it was more cost-effective; it was more efficient and practicable and faster at the end of the day. In Republika Srpska, the situation was the same. The former criminal law of the SFRY was adopted under the title the criminal law of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This may be a good moment for us to look at 4D375. This is under your tab 8. This is the law on the amendments of the criminal law of the SFRY dated 23 July 1993. This was published on the 9th of August, 1993. Let's please look at Article 1 of this law. Tell me, please, what does this law regulate? How does this relate to the things that you've just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the moment when the former law of the socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia was renamed pursuant to Article 1 to the criminal code of Republika Srpska. At the same time, some amendments were introduced to this new code, and from the point of view of my report, these amendments were not relevant. However, we can say that the monetary fines or pecuniary fines were raised because of the inflation that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? Does it mean that all the crimes that were formally envisaged by the criminal law of the SFRY were adopted by the criminal code of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Chapter 16 remained in effect in this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll do so. We have to stop here today. As I told you, there is still a long way to go. We'll reconvene Friday morning at 9.00. Is the schedule acceptable to everyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there are problems, let us know. So we stand adjourned until Friday at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.
